newsitem.title: USA: SCE&G says power plants up despite Fran.
newsitem.headline: SCE&G says power plants up despite Fran.

text.p: South Carolina Electric & Gas Co (SCE&G), citing a slight turn north by Hurricane Fran, said Thursday it now sees no need to shut its power plants.
"The hurricane's track appears to be going north of Charleston...We have not made any plans to shut down any of our plants at this time," said SCE&G spokesman Roger Schrumm.
He said this decision obviously could change depending on the path of the storm, which is expected to hit the coast near the South-North Carolina border late this evening.
SCE&G said Wednesday it anticipated having to shut its 600 megawatt, coal-fired Williams power station on Charleston Harbor as a precaution ahead of the storm.
The Williams station was damaged in September, 1989, when Hurricane Hugo hit Charleston with winds of 140 miles per hour (mph), causing about $53 million of damage to SCE&G's system.
Despite lying outside Fran's projected path, SCE&G said it expects hurricane winds (exceeding 74 mph) to sweep across parts of its service territory along the South Carolina coast.
"With this in mind, our main concern remains our transmission and distribution lines," said Schrumm.
SCE&G, a subsidiary of the SCANA Corp, provides electricity to about 500,000 customers, or 2.3 million residents, across southern and south-central South Carolina.
Earlier Thursday, Carolina Power & Light Co said it was shutting its Brunswick nuclear power facility at Southport, N.C., as a precaution ahead of Fran.
Brunswick's two units, with a combined capacity of 1,521 megawatts, lie along North Carolina's southernmost coast.
Forecasters have warned this area could bear the brunt of Fran's powerful northeast shoulder as the storm swirls ashore.
